definition: A data structure holding a fixed number of same-sized slots laid out one after another in memory. Because the slots are contiguous and equal-sized, any element can be found by arithmetic on its index. (In audio, an array instead means a group of loudspeakers or microphones used together.)
example: An array of five 4-byte integers occupies 20 consecutive bytes.

definition: Memory laid out as one unbroken block, with each item immediately after the previous one and no gaps. Arrays are contiguous; linked-list nodes generally are not.
example: A contiguous array of 1,000 doubles fills 8,000 consecutive bytes.

definition: The property that every element of an array takes the same number of bytes. Together with contiguous layout, it lets the address of any element be calculated directly from its index.
example: In an int32 array every element is exactly 4 bytes, so element 10 starts 40 bytes after element 0.

definition: A number that identifies one byte location in a computer's memory, like a house number on a very long street. (In networking, an address instead identifies a device: see IP address.)
example: If an array starts at address 1000 and holds 4-byte integers, element 2 starts at address 1008.

definition: A distance measured from a reference point, rather than an absolute position. An array index is an offset from the array's start, which is why indexing starts at 0.
example: Element 0 is at offset 0 from the start; element 3 of a 4-byte array is at a byte offset of 12.

definition: In an array, list or string, an element's position counted from the start; most languages count from 0. In databases, an index is instead a lookup structure that speeds up searches (see Database index).
example: In Python, a[0] is the first element and a[len(a) - 1] the last.

definition: Running time that does not grow with the size of the input: the operation takes about the same number of steps for 10 items or 10 million. Written O(1) in Big O notation. (In cryptography, 'constant-time' code instead means its running time does not depend on secret data, so it leaks nothing through timing.)
example: Reading a[500000] from a million-element array takes one address calculation, the same as reading a[0].

definition: Running time that grows in direct proportion to the input size n: double the input, roughly double the work. Written O(n) in Big O notation.
example: Searching an unsorted list of a million items for a value may compare all million items.

definition: Running time that grows with the square of the input size n: double the input, roughly four times the work. Written O(n²) in Big O notation. It often comes from doing O(n) work for each of n items.
example: Building a 100,000-character string one character at a time with immutable concatenation can copy about 5 billion characters.

definition: Running time that grows with the logarithm of the input size: each step typically halves what is left. Going from a thousand to a million items only doubles the work (about 10 to about 20 steps). Written O(log n).
example: Binary search finds an item among a million sorted items in about 20 comparisons.

definition: Running time proportional to n × log n: slightly worse than linear, far better than quadratic. It is the typical cost of efficient comparison sorting, such as merge sort.
example: For n = 1,000,000, n log₂ n is about 20 million, against 10¹² for n².

definition: The logarithm of n, which in algorithm analysis usually means log base 2: how many times you can halve n before reaching 1. It grows very slowly, which is why O(log n) operations stay cheap even for huge inputs.

The fixed-size block transferred or stored as a unit by a CPU cache. Line size depends on the processor and cache level. An aligned 64-byte line contains sixteen 4-byte integers or eight 8-byte doubles; the course’s numerical examples assume that width rather than a universal hardware guarantee.
example: One 64-byte cache line holds sixteen 4-byte integers or eight 8-byte doubles.

definition: When the data a program asks for is already in a cache, so it can be read quickly without going to slower memory.
example: Scanning an array sequentially gets many cache hits because each cache line serves several consecutive elements.

definition: When requested data is absent from a cache level and must come from another level or main memory. The extra cost depends on hardware, contention and the access pattern; a miss does not always mean a main-memory read.
example: Following a linked list whose nodes are scattered across memory can cause a cache miss at almost every node.

definition: The computer's primary working memory (RAM), much larger but much slower to reach than the CPU's caches.

The layering of storage from small and fast to large and slow: CPU registers, then several levels of cache, then main memory, then disk. Programs run fastest when the data they need stays near the top.

The simplified model of a computer used in algorithm analysis, where every basic operation, including reading any memory location, costs one step. It ignores caches, so two O(1) operations can differ a lot in real speed.

Processor hardware that predicts some future memory accesses, such as sequential streams, and fetches cache lines ahead of demand. Supported patterns and effectiveness vary by processor, strides, working set and contention.
example: While a loop sums an array, the prefetcher is already fetching the lines a few hundred bytes ahead.

definition: The tendency of a program to access memory locations near ones it has just accessed. Contiguous arrays have excellent spatial locality, which caches and prefetchers exploit.

A word with two unrelated meanings. (1) As a data structure, the usual meaning in algorithms, a heap is a tree kept in a special order so the smallest (or largest) item is always on top; see Binary heap. (2) In memory management, the heap is the region where a program allocates objects at run time and frees them later.
example: Python list elements are objects allocated on the heap; Python's heapq module implements the data-structure kind on a list.

definition: An array organised by row and column. A rectangular built-in C or C++ array occupies contiguous slots, with row-major ordering; other representations such as Java arrays of row arrays or NumPy strided views need not be one contiguous block.
Storing a 2D array row by row: all of row 0, then all of row 1, and so on. C, C++ and NumPy (by default) use it, so looping over columns in the inner loop walks memory sequentially.
example: In a 3 × 4 row-major grid, element (1, 0) comes straight after element (0, 3).

definition: Storing a 2D array column by column: all of column 0, then all of column 1. Fortran, MATLAB and R use it, so the fast inner loop should run down a column.
The distance in memory, in bytes, between consecutive elements a loop touches. Small strides use every byte of each cache line; large strides can touch a new cache line on every access.
example: Walking down a column of a 4,096-column row-major grid of doubles has a stride of 4,096 × 8 = 32,768 bytes.

definition: One of the oldest high-level programming languages, still used heavily in scientific computing. It stores multi-dimensional arrays in column-major order.
A commercial programming environment for numerical computing and matrix work, popular in engineering. It stores matrices in column-major order.
The reference implementation of Python, written in C, and the one most people use. Details such as list growth rates and string storage are CPython behaviour, not guarantees of the Python language.
A widely used, statically typed, object-oriented programming language that compiles to bytecode for the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
The Java Virtual Machine: the runtime that executes Java bytecode, manages memory with a garbage collector and compiles hot code to machine code just in time.
The programming language of web browsers, also used on servers (Node.js). Its strings, like Java's, are measured in UTF-16 code units.
A statically typed, object-oriented programming language from Microsoft that runs on .NET. Its strings are immutable.
A systems programming language focused on memory safety without a garbage collector. Its String type is a growable buffer of valid UTF-8.
A purely functional programming language in which values are immutable by default. Its built-in list is a singly linked list.
A family of programming languages dating from 1958, built around linked lists made of cons cells.
A programming language for the JVM that mixes object-oriented and functional styles. Its default immutable List is a singly linked list.
A language built around functions and immutable values rather than changing variables in place. Haskell, Lisp and Scala are examples.

An array that grows as you append, by allocating a bigger block, copying the elements across and freeing the old block. It tracks a length (slots in use) and a capacity (slots allocated). Python's list, Java's ArrayList and C++'s std::vector are dynamic arrays.
An array whose number of slots is set when it is created and can never change. C's int a[100] and Java's new int[100] are examples.

The most that something can hold or carry. In a dynamic array, buffer or queue it is the number of slots actually allocated, as opposed to the length (how many are in use). In a knapsack problem it is the maximum total weight, in a flow network an edge's capacity is the most flow it can carry, and in networking a link's capacity is its maximum data rate.
example: A Python list of 9 elements may have a capacity of 16, leaving 7 spare slots for future appends.

definition: The average cost per operation over a long sequence of operations, even if a few individual operations are expensive. Dynamic-array append is amortised O(1): occasional resizes copy everything, but the total over n appends is still proportional to n.
example: 17 appends to a doubling array cost 31 copies in total, under 2 per append.

definition: A sum in which each term is a fixed multiple of the one before, such as 1 + 2 + 4 + 8. When the terms shrink by a fixed factor, the sum stays within a constant multiple of the largest term, which is why multiplying an array's capacity gives amortised O(1) appends.
example: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31, just under twice the last term.

definition: A sum in which each term is a fixed amount more than the one before, such as 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n. Its total is n × (n + 1) / 2, which grows with n², so algorithms whose work forms an arithmetic series are quadratic.

The fixed factor by which a geometric dynamic-array policy multiplies capacity when it fills. A constant factor greater than one gives amortised constant-time append under the usual unit-copy model; factors nearer one retain less spare capacity but copy more in total.
example: Incremental CPython list growth is roughly 1.125; OpenJDK 21 ArrayList growth usually adds half the old capacity, subject to minimum-size and overflow rules.

definition: A value referring to a memory location or object. Conventional 64-bit CPython builds use 8-byte object pointers, but the representation and width depend on the language implementation and ABI. A Python list’s slots refer to objects stored separately.
example: A Python list holds pointers to its elements; the int objects themselves live elsewhere in memory.

definition: A value that refers to an object stored elsewhere, like a pointer that the language manages for you. Java and Python variables hold references to objects rather than the objects themselves.
example: After t = s in Python, t and s are two references to the same string object.

definition: Describes a processor and operating system whose memory addresses and general-purpose registers are 64 bits (8 bytes) wide. On such a machine a pointer usually takes 8 bytes.

A C library function that resizes a previously allocated memory block. If there is free space right after the block it can extend it in place; otherwise it allocates a new block, copies the data and frees the old one.
The function in CPython's source (Objects/listobject.c) that grows or shrinks a list's backing array. It over-allocates by about an eighth plus a few slots.
A Python function that returns the size in bytes of an object itself. For a list it includes the pointer array, so it jumps when the list's capacity grows, but not the elements the pointers refer to.
A Python standard-library type that stores numbers of one fixed type as raw machine values in a contiguous block, far more compactly than a list of int objects.
Java's standard dynamic array (java.util.ArrayList). It wraps an Object[] array and grows by about 1.5 times when full.

Wrapping a primitive value, such as a Java int, as an object reference, such as Integer, so it can be used where objects are required. Boxed objects add headers and reference access, but caching can let several boxed values share one object. ArrayList<Integer> stores references; int[] stores primitive values directly.
example: ArrayList<Integer> stores references to boxed Integer objects, while int[] stores the raw 4-byte values.

definition: A basic built-in value type, such as Java's int, long or double, stored as raw bits rather than as an object.
A language feature for writing code that works with any type, such as ArrayList<String> or ArrayList<Integer>. Java generics only accept object types, so primitives must be boxed.
A pool of pre-made Integer objects that Java reuses when boxing small values, at least −128 to 127. Values outside it normally get a new object each time they are boxed.
Bookkeeping data that a runtime such as the JVM stores at the start of every object, for things like its type and locking state. It is why a boxed Integer takes about 16 bytes to hold a 4-byte value.

A HotSpot JVM representation using 32-bit offsets for many object references in a 64-bit process. With eight-byte object alignment these can address a heap of about 32 GiB; actual use and supported sizes depend on JVM configuration and alignment, rather than every 64-bit JVM reference being four bytes.
C++'s standard dynamic array. It stores elements directly and contiguously and guarantees amortised constant-time push_back, leaving the exact growth factor to the library.
The std::vector method that appends an element at the end, reallocating to a larger block if the vector is full.
An object that walks through a collection one element at a time, remembering its position. In C++ an iterator often wraps a pointer into the container.

When a change to a container makes existing pointers, references or iterators into it unsafe to use, for example because a std::vector reallocated and moved its elements. (Cache invalidation is a different idea: marking cached data as stale.)
example: Taking &v[0], then pushing past the vector's capacity, leaves the pointer aimed at freed memory.

definition: A pointer or reference that still holds the address of memory that has been freed or moved. Using it is undefined behaviour in C and C++.
A compiler-added runtime checker that detects memory errors such as use-after-free or out-of-bounds access while a program runs. AddressSanitizer is the best known.
A dynamic array repeatedly growing and shrinking because operations alternate right at a resize boundary, so each operation pays a full copy. Shrinking only when a quarter full prevents it.
example: With doubling at full capacity and halving when at or below half full, a full 1,024-slot array can grow on push and shrink on pop repeatedly. A strictly-below-half rule needs a nearby alternating sequence; quarter-full shrinking leaves a larger gap.

definition: A check that an index lies inside an array before using it. Python and Java do it on every access and raise an error; C does not, so out-of-range access is undefined behaviour.
Reserving a block of memory for a program to use, usually from the heap. Each allocation has a time cost, and freed memory must later be reclaimed.
example: Each push onto a linked stack allocates one node; a list-based stack writes into spare capacity instead.

definition: Describes memory that a garbage collector reclaims automatically once nothing can reach it any more. Java, Python and Go are garbage-collected languages.
A unit of memory size equal to 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 bytes, slightly more than a megabyte (1,000,000 bytes).
example: A 4,096 × 4,096 grid of 8-byte doubles takes 128 MiB.

definition: One billionth of a second (10⁻⁹ s). CPU cache and memory latencies are usually quoted in nanoseconds.
A whole number stored in 32 bits (4 bytes), covering about ±2.1 billion. C's int and Java's int are usually or always this size.
A compiler optimisation that turns a loop into SIMD instructions processing several elements at once. It works best on contiguous data in the inner loop.
A compiler optimisation that swaps the order of nested loops, for example so the inner loop walks memory contiguously.
A Java library of collections specialised for primitive types, such as IntArrayList, avoiding the boxing overhead of ArrayList<Integer>.
A Java collections library that, among other things, provides primitive collections such as IntArrayList.
A Python standard-library module for binary search on a sorted list, finding where a value is or would go in O(log n) comparisons.
Python's built-in unordered collection of unique, hashable values, implemented as a hash table, so membership tests take O(1) time on average.
A set of functions callable from the C language. Passing &v[0] or v.data() is how C++ vector data is handed to such functions.
Writing past the end of an array or buffer into neighbouring memory. In C, with no bounds checks, it is a classic source of crashes and security vulnerabilities.
In programming, a sequence of text units, such as characters, code points or bytes, stored in order. Most languages implement strings on top of arrays.

A value whose observable contents cannot change after creation. Operations return a result without changing the old value; an unchanged result may reuse the old object. Strings in Python, Java, JavaScript, C# and Go are immutable.
example: In Python, s.upper() returns a new string; s itself is unchanged.

definition: Can be changed in place after it is created. Python lists and Java StringBuilders are mutable.

Associating a variable name with an object, or changing that association. After s += "x" on a Python string, other names still observe the old text. A runtime may reuse unshared internal storage when no alias can observe a mutation; rebinding does not promise a fresh allocation.
The number a hash function produces for a key. Hash tables use it to choose where to store the key, so it must never change while the key is stored.
example: Java caches a String's hash code in the object after the first hashCode() call.

definition: Python’s built-in mapping from keys to values, implemented as a hash table. Keys must be hashable: str and int qualify, and a tuple qualifies only when all its elements are hashable. A list cannot be used as a key; immutability alone does not guarantee hashability.
Java's standard hash-table map from keys to values (java.util.HashMap).
In Python, an object that has a hash value that never changes during its lifetime and can be compared for equality, so it can be a dict key or set member. Lists are deliberately unhashable.
One slot (or group of slots) in a hash table, chosen from a key's hash value. A key whose hash changed would sit in the wrong bucket and never be found.
Keeping a single shared copy of each distinct string value, so identical strings can point to the same object. It is safe only because strings are immutable.
example: Java interns string literals, so two "hello" literals refer to one object.

definition: A string written directly in source code, such as "hello".
A name in source code for a variable, function or class, such as total or is_empty.
Safe to use from several threads at the same time without corrupting data. Immutable objects are thread-safe automatically, because no thread can change them.
A bug class where something is checked (say, a file's permissions) and then used, but it changes in between. An immutable string can't change, but the file it names still can.
A rule for turning characters into bytes and back. ASCII, UTF-8 and UTF-16 are encodings; the same text can take different numbers of bytes in each.
example: "é" is 2 bytes in UTF-8 and 2 bytes (one code unit) in UTF-16; "A" is 1 byte in UTF-8.

aliases: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
definition: A 7-bit character encoding of 128 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes. Every ASCII character is one byte in UTF-8.
example: A is 65 (0x41) in ASCII.

definition: The universal character set that gives every character in the world's writing systems, plus symbols and emoji, a number called a code point. Its encodings include UTF-8 and UTF-16.
example: Unicode 15.1 (2023) defines 149,813 characters; later versions add more.

definition: The number Unicode assigns to a character, written U+ followed by hexadecimal digits. Code points run from U+0000 to U+10FFFF.
example: U+0041 is A, U+00E9 is é, U+1F600 is 😀.

definition: Any Unicode code point except the surrogate range U+D800–U+DFFF. These are the values UTF-8 is allowed to encode.
The fixed-size chunk an encoding works in: 8 bits for UTF-8, 16 bits for UTF-16. A character can take one or several code units.
example: In Java, "😀".length() is 2 because the emoji needs two UTF-16 code units.

definition: A Unicode encoding using one to four bytes for each Unicode scalar value, with ASCII values using exactly one byte. Surrogate code points are excluded from valid UTF-8. A visible grapheme cluster can contain several scalar values and therefore need more than four bytes.
example: "café" is 4 code points but 5 bytes in UTF-8, because é takes 2.

definition: A Unicode encoding using one 16-bit code unit for most common characters and a pair of them (a surrogate pair) for the rest, including most emoji. Java and JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units.
Two UTF-16 code units, one from U+D800–U+DBFF and one from U+DC00–U+DFFF, that together encode a code point above U+FFFF. Splitting a string between them produces garbage.
example: 😀 (U+1F600) is stored in UTF-16 as the pair D83D DE00.

definition: The first byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence. Its high bits say how many bytes the character uses.
example: é (U+00E9) is C3 A9 in UTF-8; C3 is the lead byte.

definition: A byte of the form 10xxxxxx that follows the lead byte in a multi-byte UTF-8 character. A lead byte without its continuation bytes is invalid UTF-8.
A one-byte character encoding covering the first 256 Unicode code points (U+0000–U+00FF): ASCII plus Western European accented letters.
A Unicode code point, such as U+0301 (combining acute accent), that attaches to the character before it instead of standing alone.
example: e followed by U+0301 displays as é but is two code points.

definition: A single code point that already includes an accent, such as é (U+00E9), as opposed to a base letter plus a combining mark.

Converting Unicode text to a specified normal form so canonically equivalent sequences compare equally, for example composing e plus U+0301 to é under NFC. It does not make every visually identical string equal: unrelated characters can look alike.
What a reader perceives as one character, which may be several code points: a letter plus accents, a flag emoji, or a family emoji joined by special characters.
example: The 🇬🇧 flag is one grapheme cluster made of two code points.

definition: Python Enhancement Proposal: a design document describing a new Python feature or convention. PEP 8 is the style guide; PEP 393 defines how CPython stores strings.
The Python Enhancement Proposal (Python 3.3) under which CPython stores each string with 1, 2 or 4 bytes per code point, chosen by its widest character, so indexing stays O(1).
example: A long ASCII string with one emoji added is stored at 4 bytes per character.

definition: Python's official style guide. Among much else, it warns not to rely on CPython's in-place string concatenation optimisation.
A Java 9 feature that stores a String in Latin-1, one byte per char, when all its characters fit, and in UTF-16 otherwise, roughly halving memory for mostly-ASCII text.
A character-sized value type. In Java a char is 16 bits (one UTF-16 code unit); in C a char is one byte, and a C string is an array of chars.
C++'s standard string type: a mutable, growable buffer of chars that owns its contents.
A lightweight, read-only window onto characters owned by some other string, so substrings can be passed around without copying. C++ has std::string_view; Rust has &str.
In C, a string is just an array of bytes ending in a zero byte ('\0'). Nothing stores its length, so finding the length means scanning for the zero.
The C library function that returns a string's length by scanning for its terminating zero byte, which takes O(n) time for n characters.
A compiler optimisation that moves a calculation whose result can't change out of a loop, so it runs once instead of every iteration ("hoisting" it).

Joining strings end to end. In a full-copy model the result copies both inputs, with work proportional to their combined length. Some runtimes can reuse or extend unshared storage while preserving observable string immutability, so allocation behaviour is implementation-dependent.
Java's mutable, growable character buffer for building strings efficiently: append pieces, then call toString() once.
The Python string method that concatenates a list of strings in one pass: it measures the total length, allocates once and copies each piece once.
example: "".join(["a", "b", "c"]) returns "abc".

definition: The standard Java compiler, which turns .java source files into JVM bytecode.

Selecting part of a sequence, such as s[2:5] in Python; a non-unit step can select nonadjacent elements. List slices produce new lists, while proper CPython string slices generally copy into new strings; an unchanged full immutable-string slice can reuse the original. Other languages can provide borrowed views.
example: s = "hello"; s[1:4] is "ell".

definition: A contiguous run of text units taken from a string, such as "ell" from "hello". Ordinary proper String.substring results in OpenJDK have copied their selected units since Java 7u6; an unchanged whole-string result can reuse the original.

Finding where one string (the needle, length m) occurs inside another (the haystack, length n). A naive search tries every starting position, O(n·m) in the worst case; cleverer algorithms run in linear time.
In substring search, the needle is the short string you are looking for and the haystack is the text you search in.
The Knuth–Morris–Pratt algorithm: a linear-time substring search that, after a mismatch, uses what it already matched to skip ahead instead of restarting.
A linear-time substring search using constant extra space, by Crochemore and Perrin (1991). CPython uses it for longer needles from Python 3.10.

Short Message Service. An ordinary single segment has up to 140 payload bytes, traditionally enough for 160 GSM 7-bit basic-alphabet characters or 70 UCS-2 code units; GSM extension characters consume two septets, concatenation reduces payload, and services that support non-BMP emoji typically use UTF-16 surrogate pairs that consume two 16-bit units.
A name–value line sent with an HTTP request or response, such as Content-Type: text/html. Servers often limit header size in bytes.

Identity asks "is this the very same object?" (Python is, Java == on objects); equality asks "do these hold the same value?" (Python ==, Java .equals()). Two different objects can be equal but not identical.
The system that runs a program and provides its built-in services, such as memory management (for example the JVM or CPython). "At runtime" also means "while the program is running".
Code that runs very often, so its speed dominates a program's performance.
A Python exception raised when an operation is applied to the wrong kind of object, such as assigning to s[0] on a string or comparing two dicts with <.
A Python exception raised when bytes cannot be decoded with the requested encoding, for example a UTF-8 sequence cut off part-way through a character.

An error signalled while a program runs that interrupts normal flow until some code handles it; unhandled, it usually ends the program with a message. Processors also raise hardware exceptions, such as page faults, which the operating system handles.
Comma-separated values: a plain-text table format with one record per line and fields separated by commas.
Short for identifier: a value that uniquely names a record, user or object.

One element of a linked structure such as a linked list, tree or graph, holding a value plus links to other nodes. In networking and distributed systems, a node instead means one device, machine or process.
example: In 3 → 8 → 5, each number lives in its own node with a pointer to the next.

definition: The first node of a linked list. The list itself is usually just a reference to its head.
A reference to the last node of a linked list. Keeping one makes appending O(1) instead of a walk from the head.
A linked list whose nodes each hold one pointer, to the next node. You can only walk it forwards, and deleting a node needs its predecessor.
A linked list whose nodes hold pointers to both the next and the previous node, so you can walk both ways and remove any node you hold in O(1).
A linked list whose last node points back to the first instead of to nothing, so traversal must stop when it returns to its starting node.

An extra marker node that is not a data element and simplifies boundary handling. A dummy head supplies a predecessor for the first element; a circular doubly linked sentinel supplies both neighbours for every data node, including when it is the only element. A sentinel value is a related marker idea; Redis Sentinel is an unrelated availability tool.
example: In a circular doubly linked list with a sentinel s, the list is empty exactly when s.next is s.

definition: A throwaway node placed before the real head of a linked list while building or editing it, so the first node needs no special case. You return dummy.next at the end.
Visiting every element of a data structure in some order, such as walking a linked list from head to tail.
The node immediately before a given node in a sequence. A singly linked list must walk from the head to find it.
The node immediately after a given node in a sequence; in a linked list, the one its next pointer points to.
A reference you keep to a specific item, such as a node, so you can find it again directly without searching.
example: An LRU cache's hash map stores a handle to each list node, giving O(1) moves to the front.

definition: Remove a node from a linked list by rewiring its neighbours' pointers to skip it.
Moving a run of nodes from one linked list into another (or elsewhere in the same list) by changing a few pointers at the boundaries, without copying.
A linked list whose next/prev pointers live inside the objects themselves, so adding an object to the list needs no separate node allocation. The Linux kernel uses them widely.
The Linux kernel's intrusive circular doubly linked list type, used with a sentinel head; list_empty tests whether the head points back to itself.
C++'s standard doubly linked list. Inserting or erasing elements never invalidates iterators to other elements.
Java's standard doubly linked list (java.util.LinkedList). Each node is an object holding the item and next and prev references; get(i) walks from the nearer end.
A Python dict subclass (collections.OrderedDict) that remembers insertion order and can move a key to either end in O(1), useful for LRU caches.
A Java hash map that also keeps its entries in a doubly linked list, preserving insertion order or (optionally) access order for LRU caches.
Taking turns in a fixed cycle, giving each participant a share before returning to the first. A circular list models it naturally.
Building a new version of an immutable data structure that reuses unchanged parts of the old one instead of copying them. Prepending to an immutable list shares the whole old list.
In Lisp and functional languages, a two-field node holding a value and a pointer to the rest of the list; it is how prepending builds lists.

Following dependent references where the next address becomes known only after the current load completes. This limits overlap of loads along that chain; other independent work can still overlap, and actual cost depends on the cache state and hardware.
A block of pre-allocated, same-sized slots handed out and returned by the program itself, avoiding a general-purpose allocation per object.
A C library function that copies a block of bytes to a possibly overlapping location. Shifting elements in a contiguous array is essentially one memmove, which runs very fast.
A node whose pointer points back to itself. In a linked list it makes any traversal loop forever.
A fixed-size cache that, when full, evicts the least recently used entry. The classic design pairs a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list kept in recency order.
Done by changing the existing data where it is stored rather than building a copy. For an algorithm, in-place usually means it rearranges its input using only O(1) extra memory.
example: Reversing a linked list in place just flips each next pointer.

definition: Memory an algorithm needs beyond its input. O(1) extra space means only a fixed handful of variables, however large the input.
A linked-list technique using two pointers that move at different speeds, typically one and two steps at a time. It finds the middle in one pass and detects cycles in O(1) memory.

An algorithm that detects a loop in a linked list with two pointers, one moving one step and the other two steps at a time; they meet if and only if there is a cycle. A second phase finds where the cycle starts.
Finding whether following pointers (or applying a function repeatedly) eventually loops back on itself, and if so where the loop starts and how long it is.
A cycle-detection algorithm by Richard Brent (1980) that, like Floyd's, uses O(1) memory but typically needs fewer pointer moves.
Arithmetic on remainders, where numbers wrap round after reaching a fixed value (the modulus), like hours on a clock. Ring buffers and cycle arguments both use it.
example: 14 o'clock is 2 o'clock on a 12-hour clock: 14 mod 12 = 2.

definition: a ≡ b (mod m), read "a is congruent to b modulo m", means a and b leave the same remainder when divided by m.
example: 7 ≡ 2 (mod 5), because both leave remainder 2.

definition: Combining two already-sorted sequences into one sorted sequence by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. It takes time proportional to their combined length.
A sorting algorithm that splits the input in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the results, taking O(n log n) time. It needs no random access, so it suits linked lists.
A sort or merge is stable if items that compare equal keep their original relative order. Merging with <= rather than < keeps it stable.
The ability to reach any element directly by its position in O(1) time, as with an array. Linked lists lack it.
A sequence that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as "racecar" or 1 → 2 → 3 → 2 → 1.

The configured limit on nested interpreter calls, inspected with sys.getrecursionlimit(). Conventional CPython builds commonly start at 1,000, but configuration and implementation matter. Exceeding it raises RecursionError; excessively raising it can still crash a process on some platforms.
The Python exception raised when the call depth exceeds the recursion limit.
An optimisation where a function call that is the very last action of a function reuses the current stack frame instead of pushing a new one. CPython does not do it.
A Python exception raised when code accesses an attribute an object doesn't have, such as None.next.
A Python exception raised when an argument has the right type but an unacceptable value, such as float("abc") or n < 1.
A Python exception raised when an index is out of range, such as popping from an empty list.
A built-in Python exception meant for arithmetic results too large to represent; the lesson's ring buffer reuses it to signal "buffer full".
A last-in, first-out (LIFO) collection: you add (push) and remove (pop) only at the top. The word also names layered software, as in "network stack", and the call stack that runs function calls.
example: Push 1, 2, 3 then pop returns 3.

definition: Last in, first out: the most recently added item is the first removed. It is how a stack behaves.
The two core stack operations: push adds an item on top; pop removes and returns the top item.
Look at the item that would be removed next (the top of a stack or front of a queue) without removing it.
The end of a stack where all pushes and pops happen. On an array-backed stack it is the end of the array; on a linked stack it is the head.
The error of popping or peeking an empty stack.
Pushing onto a full fixed-size stack, or, for the call stack, recursing so deeply that it runs out of space. Java throws StackOverflowError; native programs often crash.
The classic lock-free stack (R. Kent Treiber, 1986): a linked stack whose push and pop update the head pointer with compare-and-swap, retrying if another thread got there first.

Compare-and-swap: an atomic CPU instruction that changes a memory location to a new value only if it still holds an expected value, reporting whether it succeeded. It is the building block of most lock-free algorithms.
A lock-free bug where a value changes from A to B and back to A between a thread's read and its compare-and-swap, so the CAS wrongly succeeds even though the structure changed.
Deciding when memory removed from a concurrent data structure can be freed, without another thread still reading it. Lock-free structures need special schemes such as hazard pointers.
Java's resizable circular-array deque (java.util.ArrayDeque). It is the recommended general-purpose stack and queue in Java and rejects null elements.
Java's legacy stack class. It extends Vector, so its methods are synchronized and it exposes index access; the docs recommend Deque instead.
Java's legacy synchronized dynamic array, superseded by ArrayList.

In Java, a synchronized method or block acquires a particular monitor so threads holding that same monitor cannot execute their critical sections simultaneously. Different monitors do not exclude each other. Runtime optimisations can remove some uncontended locking overhead.
A C++ container adaptor that offers only stack operations on top of another container, std::deque by default.
In C++, a class that wraps another container and exposes a restricted interface, such as std::stack or std::queue.
A Python thread-safe stack from the queue module, with blocking put and get for passing items between threads.
The stack a running program uses to track active function calls: each call pushes a stack frame and each return pops it.
The block of call-stack memory for one function call, holding its arguments, local variables and return address.
The place in the calling code where execution continues after a function returns, saved in the stack frame.

A variable local to a function or method invocation. Conceptually its state belongs to that call; actual storage can use registers, native stack slots or runtime-managed frame/object storage rather than one universal layout.
A stack data structure the program manages itself, usually on the heap, used to replace recursion so depth is limited only by memory.
An inaccessible memory page placed just past the end of a thread's stack, so running off the end causes an immediate fault instead of silently overwriting other memory.
A crash caused by a program touching memory it isn't allowed to access, such as a guard page or freed memory.
The product of all whole numbers from 1 up to n, written n!. It is a classic example of a recursive function.
Brackets are balanced when every opener has a matching closer of the same type and they nest properly: {[()]} is balanced, ([)] is not. A stack checks it in one pass.
A tool that analyses source code for likely bugs and style problems without running it.
A program that reads text in some language (source code, JSON, XML) and works out its structure, often using a stack to track nesting.
Extensible Markup Language: a text format for structured data using nested tags such as <item>...</item>.
A value an operator acts on: in 3 + 4, the operands are 3 and 4.
Writing operators after their operands, as in 3 4 + for 3 + 4. It needs no brackets or precedence rules and is evaluated with a single stack pass. Also called Reverse Polish notation (RPN).
example: 5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 - evaluates to 14.

definition: Writing operators before their operands, as in + 3 4. Also called Polish notation.
The everyday way of writing expressions, with each operator between its operands: 3 + 4 × 2. It needs precedence rules and brackets to be unambiguous.
The rule for which operators are applied first when brackets don't say: × binds tighter than +, so 3 + 4 × 2 = 11.
For operators of equal precedence, which side groups first. Subtraction is left-associative (a − b − c = (a − b) − c); exponentiation is right-associative (2^3^2 = 2^(3^2)).
An operation is commutative if swapping its operands doesn't change the result: + and × are, − and / are not.
Edsger Dijkstra's algorithm for converting infix expressions to postfix in one pass, holding pending operators on a stack and popping them by precedence and associativity.
Dutch computer scientist (1930–2002) behind the shunting-yard algorithm, Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm and much early work on structured programming and concurrency.
A processor or virtual machine whose instructions take operands from, and push results onto, a stack, much like postfix evaluation. The JVM and CPython's bytecode interpreter work this way.
A page-description language from Adobe, used by printers, whose programs are written in postfix and run on a stack machine.
A stack kept in increasing or decreasing order by popping anything that would break the order before each push. It finds each element's nearest greater or smaller neighbour in O(n).
For each element of a sequence, the first element to its right that is larger. A monotonic stack computes all of them in O(n).
example: For [2, 1, 2, 4, 3] the answers are [4, 2, 4, −1, −1], with −1 meaning none.

definition: For each day's price, count how many consecutive days up to and including today had a price no higher. It is solved in O(n) with a monotonic stack.
A search method that builds a solution step by step and undoes the last choice (pops it) when it hits a dead end, as in maze or Sudoku solvers.
Add an item to the back of a queue.
Remove and return the item at the front of a queue. Not to be confused with a deque, a double-ended queue.
A double-ended queue, pronounced "deck": a sequence supporting O(1) insertion and removal at both ends, so it can act as a stack, a queue or both. Python's is collections.deque.
A queue with a maximum size. When full it blocks or rejects producers (or, like deque(maxlen=n), discards old items), so memory can't grow without limit. An unbounded queue has no such cap.
A number used with a bitwise operation to keep, clear or test particular bits. With a power-of-two capacity, i & (cap − 1) keeps the low bits and equals i mod cap.
example: 13 & 7 = 5, the same as 13 mod 8.

definition: An operation that compares two numbers bit by bit and produces 1 only where both bits are 1. Written & in C, Java and Python.
The Linux kernel's generic lock-free-capable ring buffer, which requires a power-of-two size so indices can wrap with a bit mask.
The open-source reference implementation of the Java platform, whose source defines the actual behaviour (such as growth rates) of Java's collections.
A high-performance inter-thread messaging library from the trading firm LMAX, built on a pre-allocated ring buffer.
In a queue-based design, producers add work items and consumers take them off and process them. The queue lets them run at different speeds.
A fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a shared queue, avoiding the cost of starting a thread per task.
A small unit of data sent across a network, with headers saying where it is going. Routers hold packets in queues while waiting to send them on.
A network device that forwards packets between networks, queueing them when the outgoing link is busy. (In web frameworks, a router instead maps URLs to handler code.)
A server that receives messages from producers, stores them (often in queues or partitioned logs) and delivers them to consumers. Kafka and RabbitMQ are examples.
In Kafka-style brokers, one ordered, append-only log that a topic is split into, so it can be spread across machines. Order is guaranteed only within a partition.
Amazon Simple Queue Service: a managed message-queue service on AWS that stores messages durably until consumers process them.
Python's thread-safe FIFO queue (queue module). With maxsize set, put blocks when it is full (or raises queue.Full if not blocking), giving backpressure.
A call that waits, pausing the thread, until it can complete, such as put on a full bounded queue.
Deliberately dropping or rejecting some work when a system is overloaded, so the rest can be served in time.
Grouping many small items into one operation to cut per-item overhead.
A set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges, used to model networks, maps and dependencies. In an unweighted graph every edge counts as length 1.
The route between two nodes of a graph with the fewest edges (unweighted) or the smallest total weight (weighted).
An algorithm for shortest paths in a graph with non-negative edge weights, which uses a priority queue to always expand the closest unfinished node next.

A window of fixed size, measured in elements or in time, that moves along a sequence so only the most recent items are considered. In algorithms it is a run of consecutive elements moving one position at a time, as in "the maximum of every 3 consecutive values"; rate limiters and TCP use related time- and byte-based windows.
example: For [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7] and size 3, the window maxima are [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7].

definition: A deque kept in increasing or decreasing order, popping from the back items that can never matter again. It gives the maximum of every sliding window in O(n) overall.
A heap where every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest item is always at the root and can be removed in O(log n).
A heap where every parent is greater than or equal to its children, so the largest item is at the root.

Python's standard-library module that keeps an ordinary list arranged as a binary min-heap: heappush adds, heappop removes the smallest and heapify builds a heap in O(n). Python 3.14 adds max-heap versions.
An ordered, immutable sequence of values, such as (2, "write report"). Python compares tuples element by element, moving to the next element only on a tie.
An extra value used to order items whose main keys are equal. A strictly increasing counter in heap entries also keeps equal priorities in arrival order.
A Python function returning an endless counter 0, 1, 2, ...; next(counter) gives the next number, handy as a unique tie-breaker.
Java's binary-heap priority queue (java.util.PriorityQueue), a min-heap by natural order unless given a Comparator. Its iterator does not visit items in priority order.
A Java object that defines how two items should be ordered, letting a collection sort by something other than their natural order.
A simulation that jumps from one scheduled event to the next in time order, kept in a priority queue keyed by event time.
The rule a heap maintains: each parent compares less than or equal to its children (min-heap) or greater than or equal (max-heap).
Memory use that grows in proportion to the input size n, such as a visited set holding every node, or one stack frame per node in a recursion.
example: Recursively reversing a 10,000-node list needs about 10,000 stack frames.

definition: Running a hash function over data to get a hash value. Hashing a string reads every character, so it costs O(n) for n characters, which is why Python and Java cache a string's hash.

A first-in, first-out (FIFO) collection: items join at the back (enqueue) and leave from the front (dequeue), like people waiting in line. Used for buffering work, breadth-first search and passing items between threads.
example: Enqueue A, B, C, then dequeue three times: you get A, B, C in that order.

definition: First in, first out: the item that has waited longest is removed first. It is how a queue behaves, the opposite of a stack's LIFO.
A fixed-size array used as a queue whose end wraps round to its start, tracked with a head index and a count (or head and tail indices). Enqueue and dequeue are O(1) and nothing is ever shifted.
example: With 4 slots, head 2 and count 2, the next item goes in slot (2 + 2) mod 4 = 0.

definition: The basic unit of computer memory: 8 bits, enough for 256 different values. Memory addresses number bytes, and sizes are counted in them.
example: A 32-bit integer takes 4 bytes; a 64-bit pointer takes 8.

definition: A binary digit, 0 or 1: the smallest unit of information. Eight bits make a byte.
example: The 4-bit pattern 1101 is 13 in decimal.

definition: Pictographs such as 😀 that are encoded as Unicode characters. Most lie above U+FFFF, so they take 4 bytes in UTF-8 and a surrogate pair (2 code units) in UTF-16; some, like flags, are several code points.
example: "😀".length is 2 in Java and JavaScript but len("😀") is 1 in Python.

definition: A Python library for numerical computing. Its ndarray represents an array with a fixed dtype, shape and strides; newly allocated numeric arrays commonly use contiguous storage, while views can be noncontiguous and object arrays store references rather than raw numeric values.
example: A NumPy array of a million 8-byte floats takes about 8 MB.

definition: The core of the Linux operating system: the program that manages memory, processes and hardware. Its source includes widely studied data structures such as struct list_head and kfifo.

In C and C++, what happens when a program breaks a language rule such as reading past the end of an array or using freed memory: the standard places no requirements on the result, so it may crash, corrupt data or appear to work.

A number of the form 2^k for a whole number k ≥ 0, that is k copies of 2 multiplied together (2^0 = 1): 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ... In binary it is a single 1 followed by zeros, which is why x mod 2^k can be computed with a bit mask.
example: 64 = 2^6 is 1000000 in binary.

definition: Base-16 notation, using the digits 0–9 and A–F; one hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits. Memory addresses and Unicode code points are usually written in hex.
example: 0x41 = 4 × 16 + 1 = 65, the ASCII code for A.

definition: The remainder left after whole-number division: 13 mod 4 = 1 because 13 = 3 × 4 + 1. Written % in Python, C and Java. It makes ring-buffer indices wrap round to 0.
A way of organising data in memory so that particular operations, such as lookup, insertion or removal, are efficient. Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are basic examples.
A type defined only by the operations it supports and how they behave, not by how it is stored. A stack is an abstract data type; an array or a linked list can implement it.

IEEE 754 binary64 floating-point format: 64 bits (8 bytes), with roughly 15–16 significant decimal digits. Java double uses this format, conventional C/C++ double implementations and CPython float do too; the C and C++ languages do not universally require double to be binary64.
A mutual-exclusion lock: a flag that only one thread can hold at a time, so code that holds it can update shared data without other threads interfering. Waiting for a lock costs time.
A compiled systems programming language derived from C, with classes and templates. Its standard library includes std::vector, std::list, std::deque and std::string.
A widely used, dynamically typed programming language. Its usual implementation, CPython, is written in C.
The software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs, sharing out the CPU, memory and devices; Linux, Windows and macOS are examples. Its scheduler decides which thread runs next.
An open-source message broker that stores messages in queues and delivers them to consumers.
Amazon Web Services: Amazon's cloud-computing platform, which offers managed services such as SQS.
A reference or pointer that deliberately points at no object (null in Java, None in Python, NULL in C). Following it is an error.
example: Java's ArrayDeque throws NullPointerException if you add null.

definition: Small, fast memory inside the processor that keeps copies of recently used data from main memory, loaded a cache line at a time. Programs that reuse nearby data run much faster because of it.

A retained reference or iterator that continues to identify an existing node while other nodes are inserted or removed. In std::list, insertion preserves existing iterators and references; erasure invalidates those for the erased elements. A stable handle does not promise bounded allocation latency or validity after its own node is removed.
example: An iterator to the middle element of a std::list stays usable after another element is inserted at the front.
